definition: In this context, mechanistic theory refers to an account of conceptual representation that explains how words and concepts are acquired by describing the processes involved, especially how they are grounded in bodily experience across external and internal modalities. It is presented as a way to explain age of acquisition beyond traditional psycholinguistic factors alone.

reasons: The packet only says the authors “present a mechanistic theory of conceptual representation” that can account for groundability and existing variables in concept acquisition; it does not support the definition’s claim that this theory specifically explains how words and concepts are acquired by detailing the processes involved.
The packet supports grounding in external and internal modalities as part of the paper’s broader argument, but not as the defining content of “mechanistic theory” itself.
The phrasing overgeneralizes the theory into a broader account of conceptual representation and embodiment than the source explicitly provides.

The packet does not state that the proposed mechanistic theory specifically “explains how words and concepts are acquired by describing the processes involved.” It only says the authors “present a mechanistic theory of conceptual representation” that can account for groundability and for variability in age of acquisition, in addition to existing variables.

The definition specifies that bodily experience is grounded “across external and internal modalities.” While the packet discusses grounding in external modalities and the importance of interoceptive/internal features, it does not directly tie this particular “mechanistic theory” to grounding across external and internal modalities in those exact terms.

The definition attributes particular explanatory scope to the mechanistic theory (“explains how words and concepts are acquired”) beyond what the packet explicitly supports, since the packet does not provide a concrete description of what processes the mechanistic theory uses to explain acquisition.
